_source.displaydescription: Taḥgaḥcībhāḥ Caitya ("Big Caitya") is located at the south-west corner of Macchindrabāhāḥ. It is the biggest caitya in this area and exhibits a style typical of the 16th century (Gutschow (2011, vol 1: 152). H. Śākya (1993, 82) describes it as a Vajradhātu caitya. The caitya is built with small traditional mā apā bricks which attests to its antiquity. The four corners, the frames around the niches and the finial are all made of stone. Statues of Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi are installed in the eastern, southern, western and northern niches of the caitya respectively. In addition, a statue of Akṣobhya is attached to the eastern plinth and an inscription has been placed on the south-eastern corner of the caitya. The inscription mentions that the caitya was renovated by five Śākyas in 1749 CE. A historical photo from 2000 (published in Buṅgamatīko Sā̃skṛtika Sampadāharū, p. 50) shows that the caitya was in a dilapidated condition. However, it was renovated in 2002. A Śākya family residing in the vicinity south of the caitya takes care of it and performs all annual rituals.

_source.displaydescription: In 1637, King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla built this pillar in collaboration with the Kṛṣṇa Temple (LAL1340). The gilded Garuḍa statue stands on an almost 7 meter tall rectangular pillar, measuring 55 x 55 cm. The 171 cm tall statue is greeting Kṛṣṇa in namaskāra gestur, and sits on a pedastal decorated with lotus petals. Whenever Kṛṣṇa is worshipped in the temple, the statue also receives some of the pūjā material, as Garuḍa is the vehicle of Viṣṇu. The image is therianthropic; half of it is in the shape of a bird, while the other half has a human appearance. Garuḍa appears in a benign posture; he is kneeling with his right knee upwards and his left knee on the pedastal as he prays to Kṛṣṇa. He is wearing a crown, and has a red ṭīkā on his forehead. Snakes adorn his neck and ears as ornaments, and he wears armlets on his wrists and arms. He has dhotī on his lower body and a girdle on his waist. Two wings and a tail can be found on his back.
_source.displayname: Garuḍa Stambha (1637 CE) || गरुड स्तम्भ || LAL1341

_source.displaydescription:
Guitaḥ Caitya 2 is located to the east of the Cīdhã Bahī (LAL1970) and to the north of the Guitaḥ Hiti. It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the four cardinal directions. The platform is paved with teliā tiles and has a stone edge. A fire alter can be found in the courtyard in front of the shrine.

The main deity is Akṣobhya and his statue has been placed in the western niche. This is unusual, as he is normally located on the eastern side of such caitya. Here, however, he faces towards the main deity in the Cīdhã Bahī. This main western niche is adorned with a stone doorframe displaying images of the Five Buddhas. The other three niches are plain and exhibit a different type of roof. The diameter of the single-plinth drum is 790 cm and the dome atop it has a diameter of 720 cm. Above the dome is a harmikā based on a square plan of 187 cm and measuring 100 cm in height. There are thirteen rectangular tiers and an āmalaka and a yaḥsĩ (central pillar) above the harmikā, and a gilded parasol has been fixed above the caitya.

A statue of Ratnasambhava undeneath five nāgas (snakes) is housed in the southern niche of the Caitya. These five nāgas intertwine to form a triangular shape above him. Amitābha is enshrined in the eastern niche and Amoghasiddhi is located in the northern one. The images of Amitābha and Ratnasambhava seem to be have been added recently. These four shrines have been topped with caitya-shaped pinnacles, though the pinnacle of the northern niche is damaged. 

The main Caitya is surrounded by four smaller khaṭa-style caityas at its four corners; this formation is known as cilãdyaḥ. These caityas have been painted with white lime and house images of Buddha. Images of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara have been enshrined inside the north-western and north-eastern caityas. An image of a six-handed deity standing on a yoni has been enshrined in the south-eastern caitya. The deity’s face, as well as the number of his hands and weapons cannot be seen clearly. He might be one of the Lokeśvaras. Inside the south-western khaṭa-shaped caitya, one can find a sitting statue of Vairocana alongside his associative deities. L. Bangdel (1995, 228) has dated the Vairocana image to around the 6th century. All four caityas have small caitya shaped pinnacles at their top. The pinnacles of the north-western and south-eastern structures have been damaged; only the āmalaka part of the remains. The thirteen tiers of the north-eastern caitya have also been lost. 

No inscription or any other documented evidence could be found to provide information about the establishment of the caitya. Since the Vairocana image on the south-western khaṭa-shaped caitya has been dated to the 6th century, it can be assumed that the main Caitya was also constructed around that time.

_source.displaydescription:
Śaṅkhadhara Bāhāḥ is an independent vihāra. The building is located on the right-hand side of the street that leads from Bhelāchẽ to Cyāsal Square, and is easily identifiable thanks to the three phalcās that surround it. One phalcā sits in front of the monument (to the west), the second is attached to the southern side of the building, and the third can be found to its north just across the street. The Bāhāḥ sits on a high plinth of 75 cm; this has been built using unusually large bricks. The decorative kasimvaḥ and libī bricks are also larger than is characteristic for a bāhāḥ. The sanctum can be accessed by climbing a series of steps that are flanked by two stone lions. The building has a single carved door on the ground floor of the main facade, which faces west. The door is guarded by a pair of terracotta serpents with a decorative brick lining.

The upper floor is separated by a band of timber cornices with a pair of lhāḥkā at each of their projected ends. On the first floor, a carved window is set in the center of the main wall and has two small blind windows on either sides. The original struts, the toraṇa and the roof structure are all missing. A new floor has been built on top of the first floor using brick masonry and mud mortar. This floor has a double-leaf glazed window. The building is now covered in corrugated metal sheets.

The front yard is paved in stone. It has a caitya (225 cm high) on a square brick base and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala lined up on its western axis.

This independent vihāra was established by Śaṅkhadhara Prajāpati in 1868 (NS 988). The carved, brass entrance of the sanctum has no toraṇa, but it does have the usual two stone lions sitting in front of it. The main image of Akṣobhya has been lost, and since then the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ has remained empty. A photo printed in Pruscha (1975, 176) shows stone pillars erected on the left-hand side of the plinth. These pillars are meant to hold a bell, however this too is missing. The pillars are also no longer there. To the left of the entrance, a small image of a four-handed Gaṇeśa has been placed in a small niche in the wall. Below this image, a stone inscription informs readers of the establishment of the Bāhāḥ. To the right of the entrance, one can find a small iamge of Kumāra riding on a peacock. An inscription mentions that Śaṅkhadhara Prajāpati established a guṭhī and provided it with land for the management of this Bāhāḥ. These days, however, the Bāhāḥ seems to be somewhat neglected. The ritual worship is also no longer performed.

_source.displaydescription:
Bāsimali Phalcā is located to the northwest of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and lies between Dhvākhā Phalcā and Āratī Chẽ. There are more than half a dozen phalcās in the courtyard of this temple. Many of the social-cultural activities related to Karuṇāmaya are organised in the locality, and these phalcās were constructed as sites within which to hold such activities. This three-bayed phalcā is located on the ground floor of a three-storey building. The roof of the building is supported by six carved struts and is covered with corrugated metal sheets. The second storey has a three-bayed window.

The construction of this phalcā was facilitated by a Tāmrākāra family from Cāsukhela, Bhaktapur in 1868 CE. Originally, the building was called satala. Its founders had established a guṭhī for its management. However, the building collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was reconstructed by the desecendents of the founders in 1942. A historical photo taken around 1968 shows that the building once had a jhĩgaṭī-tiled roof and a traditional window (Bungamati 1968, 21). The Bāsimali Phalcā collapsed again in 2001 and in the same year Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra, another descendent of the founders, took on the task of renovating it. Once the renovations were complete, she deposited a lump sum of money in the bank to allow for the continuation and management of bhajana chanting in Bāsimali Phalcā.

A statue of Vāsuki Nāga and a lion are attached to the inner wall of the phalcā. Locals worship Vāsuki as Viṣṇu and the lion as Garuḍa.

Nārāyaṇadevī Tāmrākāra also donated musical instruments to a bhajana group in 2001, and this group now performs bhajana during the months of Gũlā and Kārttika. A group of yogin returns here after taking part in the Hariśaṅkara procession of Pharping before proceeding on to the Paśupatinātha Temple to perform Jogīcakra Pūjā. Upon returning from Pharping, the yogins carry a thick roṭī on their head which is tied and fixed in place by knots made by their matted hair. They rest for a while in Bāsimali Phalcā and offer the roṭīs to Karuṇāmaya. Afterwards, they distribute the remaining roṭī to the public as the gift of the deity. Some of the locals claim that the stale mali (Nep. roṭī) was distributed in the phalcā, and that this is how the monument got its name.
